### Agostini v. Felton and Chancellor, Board of Education of the City of New York v. Felton, Nos. 96-552 and 96-553

Merits decision, June 23, 1997

#### Chronology and Posture

Agostini v. Felton, No. 96-552, consolidated with Chancellor, Board of Education of the City of New York v. Felton, No. 96-553. Decided June 23, 1997. Argued April 15, 1997, on writs of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.

The Board and a new group of parents filed motions for Rule 60 relief in October and December 1995. On August 7, 1996, the Second Circuit affirmed denial of relief from the September 26, 1985 permanent injunction implementing Aguilar. The question under Rule 60(b)(5) is whether that continuing onsite prohibition should remain in light of the governing Establishment Clause law and the preserved request to reconsider Aguilar. The two dockets concern the same prospective injunction and share one decision. Public teachers provide supplementary secular Title I instruction to independently eligible children under public control; the injunction requires offsite delivery.

All nine Justices participated at argument and decision.

#### Judgment

**Vacated and remanded in both consolidated dockets, 5–4.**

**Supporting:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas.
**Opposing:** Justices Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The Second Circuit judgments affirming denial of relief are vacated. Proceedings return for a district-court order removing the injunction's onsite prohibition to the extent it rests on the categorical ground rejected today. Any genuinely independent basis must be identified and decided under the surviving law; absent such a basis the prohibition must be dissolved. The City must obey the operative decree until judicial modification. Existing lawful services may continue during prompt implementation, and children currently receiving them should continue to receive them with existing statutory duties preserved. No new service entitlement, fixed timetable, damages or repayment is imposed.

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I–IV | Stone-Zsela | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas in full | Vacate both judgments and remand for tailored prospective relief | Part I: modification of Lemon; Part II: onsite secular-service rule and precise overruling; Part III: present legal change under Rule 60(b)(5); Part IV: tailored removal with retained safeguards and lawful obligations |
| Dissent, Part I | Souter | Stevens and Ginsburg | Would affirm both judgments | Affirmative substantive objection to this public instructional support; Breyer does not join |
| Same dissent, Part II | Souter | Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer | Would affirm both judgments | Retention of precedent and absence of sufficient intervening erosion or factual change |
| Dissent | Ginsburg | Stevens, Souter and Breyer | Would affirm both judgments on an independent procedural ground | Rule 60 review cannot supply this means of rehearing the original constitutional ruling |

#### Holdings

All four holdings are delivered by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela in the Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas. Each has five direct joins at its stated level of generality, including the modification of Lemon in Holding I. No aggregation of separate opinions supplies controlling authority.

##### I. Lemon governs through one inquiry into governmental religious authority and function

**Holding and operative rule:** Lemon remains the governing Establishment Clause test, modified so that purpose, effects and entanglement are evidence within one inquiry: a specific prohibition or distinct doctrine controls when it resolves the conduct; an established permissible relationship defeats the claim on that ground; otherwise a legally sufficient unresolved allegation is decided through attribution and function under ordinary procedure. These are three routes within the updated Lemon test, not freestanding prongs, exemptions from review or an alternative test for uncertain cases.

**Authority:** Part I of the Opinion of the Court; Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas join this modification in full, supplying five direct joins at this level of generality.

**Operative qualifications:** The court identifies the governmental act—an official message, organized event, exercise of supervisory power or expenditure—and the function it performs. For financing, the question is what government purchases or performs; all religious conduct of the recipient need not become government speech. Private-access authorization, religious identity and physical location are relevant in context but are not individually decisive.

Government may not organize worship as its own activity, prescribe religious profession or observance, adopt doctrine as governmental truth, solicit religious adherence through public authority, govern theology or confer civil authority on a religious basis. Denominational classifications retain their distinct strict-scrutiny rule. Independently identifiable secular work in a religious setting may be purchased with enforceable controls against devotional use and diversion. Restoration of private exercise restricted by custody or comparable governmental control remains subject to the applicable accommodation inquiry, not an automatic financing prohibition. Those distinct doctrines retain their own sources and burdens.

**Controlling explanation:** Lemon addresses governmental sponsorship of religion, financing of religious functions and the improper union of civil and religious authority. Its method must identify those acts rather than condemn an independently secular service because officials supervise it to remain secular. Aguilar exposes that defect: location and repeated contact become substitutes for examining what the public program actually does. The Court therefore modifies Lemon's operation while retaining its constitutional concerns.

Purpose and effects help identify the governmental function; institutional relationships show who directs it. Once prohibited conduct is established, actual conversion, religious success or a completed penalty is unnecessary. A secular objective cannot justify prohibited religious means. Conversely, a provider's religious motivation does not make its secular work devotional. Ordinary monitoring of secular performance is not itself establishment, even when repeated; civil control of doctrine and religious control of public authority remain forbidden.

This method requires real operational separation and reliable accountability for funded work, but not invariably separate institutional governance or wholly distinct personnel. Shared structures cannot excuse devotional financing, and they do not automatically defeat a genuinely severable public service. Here public selection, staffing, materials and supervision identify the remedial service to be examined. The school's entire religious mission is not the governmental act.

The dissent's institutional-support objection warrants scrutiny of the service, not a presumption that its secular and religious functions are inseparable. Existing specific holdings continue to govern their established relationships: Kiryas Joel restricts denominational allocation of civil power; Rosenberger permits its controlled publication benefit; Pinette and Chabad distinguish private expression and governmental attribution. The Court does not decide absent voucher, monument, legislative-prayer or accommodation programs, or declare every future application compatible with every preserved precedent.

**Precedent treatment:** Lemon v. Kurtzman remains governing, with its independent purpose, primary-effect and excessive-entanglement prongs modified into the three routes of this single inquiry. The actual holdings of Kiryas Joel, Rosenberger, Pinette, Chabad, Witters and Mueller remain in force; Zobrest supplies no Establishment Clause merits holding.

##### II. Separately administered secular instruction is not forbidden because of its religious-school location

**Holding and operative rule:** The Establishment Clause permits the described supplementary Title I service for children independently selected under neutral public eligibility criteria, delivered by public employees under public supervision with public secular materials, without religious instruction, team teaching or other cooperative instructional activity with religious-school teachers, or participation in worship, and with effective controls against diversion. Religious-school location, presumed inculcation arising from that location, incidental benefit to the school, and ordinary monitoring of that separately administered public service do not by themselves establish unconstitutional sponsorship, devotional financing or institutional control; Aguilar's categorical prohibition and Ball's corresponding Shared Time rationale are displaced at that scope.

**Authority:** Part II of the Court's opinion; the five-Justice coalition stated above directly joins the rule, its secular-control qualifications and its precise treatment of precedent.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that the constitutional inquiry must distinguish the public remedial service from the religious school's own instruction. Lemon, as updated in Part I, identifies the governmental act and its religious or secular function, using purpose, effects and institutional relationships as evidence within that inquiry. Here the remedial purpose, independent selection of eligible children, public staffing and supervision, secular materials and restrictions on religious participation identify a supplementary public service. Those safeguards establish this program's severable secular operation; operational separation and reliable accountability do not invariably require wholly distinct personnel or separate institutional governance. Ordinary consultation about a child's secular educational needs is distinct from joint teaching. Neutral eligibility or public employment alone would not excuse devotional instruction or diversion.

Aguilar treated the supervision needed to preserve secular instruction as a reason to prohibit the instruction on religious premises. That categorical inference is unsound: supervising public teachers' secular work is not, without more, governing the school's religious affairs. The absence of a finding of indoctrination does not prove every possible defect absent, but location cannot substitute for the connection between the challenged public service and an actual constitutional objection. Nor does an incidental institutional benefit alone turn this separately controlled service into religious teaching.

These safeguards existed when Aguilar was decided. The legal defect is the categorical inference that confuses secular supervision with religious sponsorship and control, not a newly discovered factual transformation. Continuing expense and impaired access make the consequence substantial; they are not the constitutional rule. Property, contractual, completed-transaction and educational-service interests receive their actual weight. No identified concrete property or completed-transaction entitlement requires retaining the categorical ban; established obligations and service continuity remain protected in implementation. Ball's Shared Time program implicated the corresponding inference about supplementary public teaching. Its distinct Community Education program predominantly used religious-school teachers and principals, and today's holding neither approves that arrangement nor reopens its judgment. The onsite rule applies Lemon as modified in Part I; the Court does not approve every program considered in Ball or reopen its completed judgment.

**Precedent treatment:** Aguilar v. Felton is overruled as authority for categorically excluding this safeguarded public Title I service from religious-school premises. School District of Grand Rapids v. Ball loses its contrary Shared Time rationale at the same scope; its Community Education judgment and unaddressed grounds remain undisturbed. Lemon v. Kurtzman governs through the updated inquiry stated in Holding I.

##### III. The Court's present change supplies the legal change required for prospective relief

**Holding and operative rule:** When this Court expressly removes the constitutional premise supporting a continuing adjudicated injunction, that present change is a significant change in law under Rule 60(b)(5), and continued categorical enforcement on the displaced premise is inequitable. The Court may apply its ruling in the pending review of denied prospective relief without requiring a second motion merely to invoke the rule it has just announced; lower courts remain bound by directly controlling precedent until this Court changes it.

**Authority:** Part III of the Court's opinion; the same five Justices directly join the present-change rule and its distinction between this continuing decree and a completed judgment.

**Controlling explanation:** Denial of Rule 60(b)(5) relief is reviewed for abuse of discretion, with its governing legal premises reviewed as questions of law. Rufo requires a significant change making continued enforcement inequitable and a modification fitted to that change. The legal change here is the Court's ruling today. It is not the expectation that the Court might reconsider Aguilar, an increase in the expense of compliance, or a supposed earlier overruling. Kiryas Joel expressly preserved Aguilar and Ball. Zobrest decided antecedent statutory and regulatory questions without deciding establishment. Rosenberger's actual printing benefit and Pinette and Chabad's private-expression holdings did not authorize this public teaching program. Rodriguez de Quijas required the lower courts to apply the directly governing rule.

The objection that Rule 60 review cannot become an untimely rehearing of the original judgment does not bar this relief. The motion addresses the decree's continuing prospective operation, and the preserved question presents the constitutional rule supporting that operation. The Court changes that rule expressly; it does not hold that the district court should have anticipated the change. Requiring a new motion solely to invoke today's decision would preserve a now-rejected prohibition without a remaining legal reason.

Rufo's limits remain. Dissatisfaction, a cheaper lawful alternative and anticipated doctrinal change are insufficient. Actual anticipation and acceptance of a risk can impose a heavy burden, but mere foreseeability is not an absolute bar and an unforeseeable catastrophe is unnecessary. A clarification of constitutional permission does not automatically erase a voluntarily accepted stricter consent obligation. This injunction enforces an adjudicated constitutional prohibition; the record establishes no negotiated promise independently requiring that prohibition. The Court neither reopens completed claims nor finds an independently sufficient factual change in costs.

**Precedent treatment:** Rufo v. Inmates of Suffolk County Jail is applied to the present legal change and retained in its significant-change, accepted-risk and tailored-relief requirements. Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/American Express, Inc. is applied to preserve lower-court obedience to direct precedent. Browder v. Director, Department of Corrections does not foreclose adjustment of continuing relief on the basis of the legal change actually adopted here; its limit on using a Rule 60 appeal to reopen the underlying completed judgment remains.

##### IV. Relief must remove the rejected prohibition while preserving independently lawful obligations

**Holding and operative rule:** On remand the district court must remove the injunction's prohibition of the described secular Title I service insofar as that prohibition rests on religious location, presumed inculcation from location or ordinary supervision of public personnel; if no independently supported legal basis sustains the onsite prohibition, it must be dissolved. Any remaining obligation must have an identified lawful basis, and any further proceedings must concern a specified material issue under the surviving law rather than require proof that future misconduct is impossible.

**Authority:** Part IV of the Court's opinion; the same five Justices directly join this tailored relief and its public-control limits.

**Controlling explanation:** Rufo connects modification to the proven change while preserving the lawful purposes of continuing relief. The change today eliminates the categorical site-and-monitoring ground. The district court therefore cannot simply reinstate that same ground, presume that public service and religious instruction are inseparable, or treat ordinary secular supervision as itself forbidden. It must remove the prohibition to that extent. Supported questions about actual religious instruction, diversion, religious control of public employees or another independent legal prohibition remain subject to ordinary procedure and the governing law; hypothetical misconduct does not justify preserving Aguilar's rejected inference.

No additional negotiated obligation is presumed. If an independent statutory, contractual or decree obligation is established, constitutional permission does not by itself extinguish it. Existing lawful services may continue while the mandate is implemented promptly. Children currently receiving those services should continue to receive them during implementation, with existing statutory duties preserved and no new service entitlement created. Any implementation period must address identified tasks and circumstances; the Court sets no number of days, and administrative delay cannot indefinitely preserve the rejected categorical prohibition. The district court modifies the decree under the mandate. Until it acts, the City must obey the operative injunction.

The holding permits the described program; it does not command onsite delivery, create an unconditional funding entitlement, approve a replacement program, award damages or repayment, cancel contracts, or excuse past disobedience. It makes no finding that every present implementation satisfies the required secular controls.

**Precedent treatment:** Rufo's suitable-tailoring requirement controls implementation and preserves any independently lawful obligation. Its consent-decree rule is not converted into a presumption that this adjudicated injunction contains a voluntary stricter undertaking.

#### Precedent Treatment

| Authority | Treatment and present force |
|---|---|
| Aguilar v. Felton, 473 U.S. 402 | Overruled as the basis for a categorical onsite prohibition on the described publicly controlled secular Title I service. No reopening of completed claims or authorization of religious instruction follows. |
| School District of Grand Rapids v. Ball, 473 U.S. 373 | Its corresponding Shared Time rationale is displaced insofar as religious location, presumed inculcation, incidental school benefit or ordinary secular monitoring categorically condemns the separately administered public service. Community Education and unaddressed holdings remain undisturbed. |
| Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U.S. 602 | Retained as the governing test, with purpose, effects and entanglement serving as evidence within one inquiry. A specific prohibition or distinct doctrine controls; an established permissible relationship defeats the claim on that ground; otherwise attribution and function resolve a legally sufficient unresolved allegation under ordinary procedure. Independent prongs and an alternative fallback inquiry no longer govern. |
| Rufo v. Inmates of Suffolk County Jail, 502 U.S. 367 | Applied to the significant legal change made today and to responsive prospective modification; accepted-risk, lawful-purpose and voluntarily accepted stricter-obligation limits remain. |
| Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/American Express, Inc., 490 U.S. 477 | Applied: directly controlling Supreme Court precedent binds lower courts until this Court changes it. |
| Browder v. Director, Department of Corrections, 434 U.S. 257 | Its limitation on review of the original judgment is distinguished from relief directed to this decree's future operation after today's legal change. |
| Board of Education of Kiryas Joel Village School District v. Grumet | Its denominational-allocation and accommodation holdings remain intact. Its preservation of Aguilar and Ball establishes the rule entering this decision, not a bar to the Court's express overruling here. |
| Zobrest v. Catalina Foothills School District | Its antecedent-law remand remains; it supplied no Establishment Clause merits holding and did not already undermine Aguilar by such a holding. |
| Rosenberger v. Rector and Visitors of the University of Virginia | Its actual controlled vendor-funded printing benefit remains permissible on its program terms. It concerns financing, not merely facility access; it neither decided this public-teaching case nor authorized every devotional expenditure. |
| Capitol Square Review and Advisory Board v. Pinette | Its bounded private-expression and access holding remains; it supplies no universal forum immunity or automatic attribution from location. |
| Chabad-Lubavitch of Georgia v. Miller | Its contextual-attribution and access holding remains; location alone does not establish governmental sponsorship. |
| Witters v. Washington Department of Services for the Blind | Its actual benefit holding remains in force; no absent tuition-voucher or provider-redemption scheme is decided. |
| Mueller v. Allen | Its actual tax-benefit holding remains in force; the Court does not decide an absent funding program or silently enlarge or displace that holding. |

#### Law After Decision

Effective June 23, 1997, Lemon remains the governing Establishment Clause test as modified in Holding I. Purpose, effects and entanglement inform a single inquiry with three routes: controlling specific prohibition or distinct doctrine, established permissible relationship, and residual attribution and function. Clear cases apply that test; its former independent prongs do not remain a separate or fallback method.

Aguilar no longer supplies a categorical constitutional bar to the separately administered, safeguarded public Title I service described in Holding II, and Ball's corresponding Shared Time rationale has no contrary force at that scope. Ball's completed judgment, Community Education and unaddressed holdings remain undisturbed. Independent prohibitions on governmental worship, devotional financing and improper institutional control remain; public employment and neutral eligibility do not immunize supported devotional conduct.

For this continuing injunction, the Court's substantive change satisfies Rule 60(b)(5)'s legal-change requirement. Removal of the now-unsupported onsite prohibition must follow through a tailored district-court order. Rufo's other requirements and Rodriguez de Quijas's rule for lower courts remain. Permission to provide the service is distinct from a statutory duty or funding entitlement. Absence of reported misconduct is not proof that every possible defect has been disproved.

The Court decides no tuition-voucher or provider-redemption scheme, monument, legislative-prayer program, general accommodation rule or all forms of direct aid. Parental selection does not itself answer what a particular expenditure purchases; no conclusion about an absent program displaces Witters or Mueller. Rosenberger remains a permissible financing arrangement on its actual controlled vendor-funded publication terms, not merely an access decision, and religious editorial viewpoint there is not automatically purchased devotional instruction. Kiryas Joel, Pinette and Chabad retain their actual holdings. Private speech, free exercise, institutional religious autonomy, denominational scrutiny and accommodation retain their distinct sources and burdens. Zobrest remains an antecedent-law remand without an Establishment Clause merits holding. No controlling rationale is drawn from separate opinions under Marks.

#### Separate Writings

##### Justice Souter, dissenting

Stevens and Ginsburg join the dissent in full. Breyer joins Part II only.

In Part I, Souter, Stevens and Ginsburg would retain Aguilar's and Ball's applicable substantive rules. Public employees conducting education within a religious school's ordinary instructional setting supply governmental educational support, not independently attributable private speech. Public staffing, neutral eligibility and safeguards do not alone resolve the institutional subsidy and entanglement concerns. Rosenberger's private publication and the private-forum decisions therefore do not decide this case. They reject the Court's modification of Lemon because its treatment of purpose, effects and entanglement within attribution and function understates the constitutional significance of continuing public instructional support. Their objection concerns this governmental program rather than a claim that every private religious act must become government speech. These Justices do not find proved proselytizing and do not require it for their structural objection. Breyer does not join this affirmative direct-aid rationale.

In Part II, all four dissenters would adhere to the direct precedents. The safeguards and anticipated costs did not newly arise. Kiryas Joel preserved Aguilar and Ball, Zobrest supplied no establishment merits holding, and the bounded expression decisions did not erode the public-instruction rule sufficiently to justify its abandonment. They oppose adopting the general methodological change as a basis for abandoning these precedents in this case. They would affirm denial of relief and preserve the injunction.

##### Justice Ginsburg, dissenting; joined by Stevens, Souter and Breyer

The four dissenters would also affirm on an independent procedural ground. Browder limits an appeal from denial of Rule 60 relief; it does not reopen the original judgment for indefinite rehearing. The district court followed still-binding Aguilar, and Rufo requires a qualifying change rather than an appeal whose own desired outcome creates the prerequisite for reopening. This Court may examine the continued force of its precedents in a proper case, but that power does not establish this vehicle's propriety. Their position does not turn an adjudicated injunction into a negotiated consent promise, deny Rule 60 relief after an actual qualifying change, or treat costs alone as sufficient. The Court's adoption of an updated Lemon test does not, in their view, cure that procedural defect. This writing addresses the route to relief independently of the substantive merits disagreement.

#### Source Notes

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(5); Felton v. Secretary, United States Department of Education, 101 F.3d 1394; the original September 26, 1985 injunction; and the original program record, including the defendants' joint statement, paragraphs 63–74, support the described posture and safeguards. That original account is not a finding that every present implementation complies. The record identifies no finding of actual indoctrination, transfer of public funds to a religious school or religious control of the public teachers; absence of such a finding is not proof that every possible defect has been disproved. The cited prior decisions supply the authority and limits stated above.

#### Mandate, Remedy, and Stage

The Supreme Court merits proceedings are complete. Both consolidated cases return through the Second Circuit for district-court implementation under Rule 60(b)(5). The next act is a judicial order removing the categorical onsite prohibition and resolving any specified, independently supported legal ground for a remaining obligation. The mandate does not itself authorize disobedience of the operative decree. Existing lawful services may continue while identified implementation tasks are completed promptly, and children currently receiving them should continue to receive them under preserved statutory duties. This creates no new service entitlement; administrative delay may not indefinitely retain the rejected prohibition. No broader delivery program or expenditure is ordered.

**End of entry: Agostini v. Felton and Chancellor, Board of Education of the City of New York v. Felton, merits decision, June 23, 1997.**

---

### Raines v. Byrd, No. 96-1671

Merits decision, June 26, 1997

#### Chronology and Posture

Argued May 27, 1997; decided June 26, 1997. On direct appeal under 2 U.S.C. §692(b) from the judgment of a single District Judge for the District of Columbia, reported at 956 F. Supp. 25. The questions are whether six Members of Congress have Article III standing and, only if they do, whether the Line Item Veto Act violates Article I's lawmaking requirements or nondelegation principles.

The Act was enacted April 9, 1996, effective January 1, 1997; the Members sued January 2. The District Court found standing and ripeness and declared the Act unconstitutional on April 10; appeal followed April 11. Four Senators and two Representatives had voted against the Act. Their votes were counted, no cancellation had injured them personally, and neither House authorized them to represent Congress. The congressional amici defended the Act's validity without taking a standing position. Senator Hatfield subsequently retired; five plaintiffs remained Members.

All nine Justices participated at argument and decision.

#### Judgment

**Vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of Article III standing, 7–2.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg.

**Opposing:** Stevens and Breyer.

Stevens would affirm the constitutional declaration. Breyer would recognize jurisdiction and proceed to the merits, which he reserves. Souter's judgment support does not join the principal injury analysis.

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Scalia | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg | Vacatur and jurisdictional dismissal | Entire opinion |
| Concurrence in the judgment | Souter | Ginsburg | Same disposition, separate Article III ground | Entire concurrence; Ginsburg also joins the Court opinion |
| Dissent | Stevens | Author alone | Would affirm the District Court | Standing, ripeness and Article I merits |
| Dissent | Breyer | Author alone | Would reject jurisdictional dismissal | Standing and ripeness; merits expressly reserved |

#### Controlling Propositions and Authority

##### I. These individual legislators lack a concrete personal injury

**Holding and operative rule:** Individual Members of Congress whose votes were counted and given full effect lack Article III standing to challenge the Line Item Veto Act on the asserted abstract dilution of Congress's institutional power and alteration of future votes. Express statutory permission to sue removes the applicable prudential obstacle but cannot supply the missing concrete personal injury.

**Authority:** The six-Justice opinion of the Court identified above adopts this rule, its explanation, limits and remedy. Souter supplies a seventh judgment vote on a separate ground.

**Controlling explanation:** Lujan requires a plaintiff's own concrete injury, with causation and redressability; legislative permission cannot replace that constitutional stake. These Members cast fully effective votes against the Act and lost. They retain office and their voting entitlement, apart from Hatfield's subsequent retirement, and identify no cancellation injuring them personally. Powell concerned exclusion from a seat, an individual deprivation absent here. Coleman concerned complete nullification of votes sufficient to determine a legislative outcome; it does not turn every change in the practical force of future votes into that injury.

Akins establishes that numerical sharing does not make a concrete deprivation abstract. Its voters were denied particular information useful to their own electoral participation. These Members instead assert an institutional allocation of power. Their strongest argument is that cancellation authority presently deprives them of voting on the ultimate legal text. But no vote of theirs was overridden or denied legal effect; the asserted change belongs to the legislative institution, which has not authorized their representation. Available legislative remedies and a later concrete cancellation controversy reinforce this bounded conclusion. They create no legislative-exhaustion requirement and do not guarantee any future plaintiff standing. The Court decides no universal rule against official injury or legislator litigation.

##### II. The jurisdictional defect requires vacatur and dismissal

**Holding and operative rule:** Because these plaintiffs lack Article III standing, the District Court's constitutional declaration must be vacated and the complaint dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. The Court does not decide the Act's constitutionality, nondelegation, Presentment or the independent ripeness question.

**Authority:** The same six-Justice Court opinion controls the jurisdictional disposition and its limits; Souter separately agrees with vacatur and dismissal.

**Controlling explanation:** Steel Co. requires resolution of disputed Article III power before disputed constitutional merits in this setting. Congress's special direct-review and expedition provisions supply a route for review, not jurisdiction over an uninjured plaintiff's constitutional complaint. Vacating the declaration removes a merits judgment the District Court lacked power to enter; it does not sustain the Act on its merits. Personal exclusion, lost salary, complete nullification of decisive votes, an authorized institutional suit meeting Article III, and an actual cancellation causing concrete injury remain distinct questions. The Court neither adjudicates any such future controversy nor adds an independent holding on traceability.

#### Precedent Treatment

- Lujan supplies the concrete-personal-injury requirement and the distinction between statutory permission and constitutional injury; its rule is applied without enlarging its noncontrolling redressability analysis.
- Akins preserves standing for concrete injury shared by many; its informational deprivation is distinguished from the institutional dilution alleged here.
- Powell remains authority for personal exclusion from office, a circumstance not presented.
- Coleman remains authority for complete nullification of decisive votes; it is distinguished from votes counted and lost.
- Steel Co. supplies the requirement to decide disputed Article III power before the disputed merits in this setting.
- Bender and Allen support the distinction between an individual's legally cognizable stake and unauthorized institutional litigation and the separation-of-powers limits on jurisdiction. No precedent is overruled.

#### Law After Decision

These individual legislators cannot invoke Article III on this institutional-dilution claim. Congress's authorization and expedition provisions do not change that conclusion. The Act's constitutional validity remains undecided, and concrete personal or properly authorized institutional injuries remain subject to their own jurisdictional analysis.

#### Separate Positions Relevant to the Decision

**Souter, concurring in the judgment, joined by Ginsburg.** Official injury is not categorically excluded by Article III: Coleman and authorized institutional representation prevent that shortcut. Whether this injury is personal rather than official, or concrete rather than abstract, is fairly debatable. Souter instead gives decisive weight to Allen's separation-of-powers foundation and Valley Forge's restraint against unnecessary constitutional adjudication. The Members seek judicial intervention in an unauthorized internal and interbranch contest, while a beneficiary deprived of an actual spending or tax benefit may present a conventional controversy satisfying injury, causation and redressability. These conditions make the present claim constitutionally insufficient. This is neither prudential abstention, an absolute political-question bar, nor a universal requirement that another plaintiff exist.

**Stevens, dissenting.** A Member's opportunity to vote on the law's ultimate text is an individual constitutional function. The Act's present alteration of that function is concrete without waiting for a particular cancellation; Coleman supports protection of official voting power, and Bender's prohibition on unauthorized representation does not defeat a Member's own injury. Stevens finds the claim ripe and would affirm the declaration on Article I grounds. The Act permits the President, after a bill becomes law, to cancel in whole a defined discretionary dollar amount, new-direct-spending item or limited tax benefit under its conditions. Chadha requires bicameralism and presentment for repeal. Giving cancellation a different name or intelligible standards does not turn removal of enacted legal force into execution; Field's contingent execution and ordinary impoundment do not answer the distinct spending-obligation and tax effects. His ground is allocation of lawmaking authority, not a finding that the delegation's standards are insufficiently intelligible. He adds no private presidential-reservation theory and decides no later cancellation remedy.

The cancellation permission requires determinations that the action reduces the deficit, does not impair essential Government functions and does not harm the national interest; the special message must be sent within five calendar days excluding Sundays. Cancellation takes effect upon both Houses' receipt; enacted disapproval nullifies it and restores the provision from its original effective date. A disapproval bill cannot itself be canceled. Disapproval requires legislation, and the special procedures do not abolish ordinary later legislation. The Act has no force or effect on or after January 1, 2005. None of these limitations, in Stevens's view, changes the Article I character of a repeal after enactment.

**Breyer, dissenting.** The systematic impairment of the Members' existing constitutional work is sufficiently concrete. Coleman does not limit official injury to one decisive voting event, and express congressional authorization removes a prudential barrier while reducing separation-of-powers concerns; it does not enlarge Article III. The prospect of a later private suit cannot erase present injury if that injury exists. Breyer finds standing and ripeness and would proceed to the merits. He expressly reserves the Act's constitutionality and does not join Stevens's merits conclusion or vote to sustain the Act.

#### Source Notes

The Line Item Veto Act is Pub. L. 104-130, April 9, 1996, 110 Stat. 1200, including the special direct-appeal provision in §3. The single-judge judgment and notice of appeal establish the review posture. No actual cancellation or resulting private injury is found. Statutory authority: [enacted Act](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-104publ130/html/PLAW-104publ130.htm).

#### Mandate, Remedy, and Stage

The constitutional declaration is vacated. The case returns to the District Court with instructions to dismiss the complaint for lack of jurisdiction. No merits remand, injunction, cancellation adjudication or new deadline is ordered.

**End of entry: Raines v. Byrd, merits decision, June 26, 1997.**

---

### Libertarian Party of Florida v. Smith, No. 96-1867

Plenary merits decision on submission, September 21, 1998

#### Chronology and Posture

Review under 28 U.S.C. §1257 of the Florida Supreme Court's December 5, 1996 judgment, 687 So. 2d 1292, with rehearing denied February 17, 1997, approving the First District's judgment sustaining the filing-fee allocation. No exact oral-argument date in this Court is established.

The question is whether Florida Statutes §99.103(1) (1993) violates federal political-association and equality protections by distributing approximately half of qualifying parties' candidates' filing fees to those parties' executive committees for party expenses, while excluding parties below five percent of the State's registered voters. The criterion is objective and potentially changing; it does not name the Democratic and Republican Parties. The published description supports that approximate allocation, not an exact dollar formula.

The Libertarian Party, its executive committee and House candidate Wilson sought declaratory and injunctive relief. Wilson had qualified for the ballot; the parties concede the underlying candidate fees were lawfully collected. The challenged provision does not deny ballot access or restrict private political spending. No finding establishes that minor-party fees were specially exacted for, or directly transferred to, rival parties. The Florida Supreme Court treated the relevant state constitutional protection as coextensive with the federal protection in this case.

All nine Justices participate.

#### Judgment

**Affirmed, 8–1.**

**Supporting:** Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Opposing:** Stone-Zsela, who would reverse and remand for an orderly end to distributions under the challenged classification while leaving Florida a lawful fiscal choice.

No rebate, refund, repayment of completed distributions or substitute allocation formula is ordered. No candidate-access requirement or conceded lawful collection of filing fees is adjudicated.

#### Opinion Topology

Stevens delivers the Opinion of the Court, Parts I–III, joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All eight join federal review, the bounded objective-support subsidy rationale, and affirmance without a monetary or allocation order. Stone-Zsela dissents alone and would invalidate the classification and remand, without an equal-subsidy entitlement or repayment order.

Scalia and Thomas join the narrower sufficient Court rationale despite their broader views about subsidies. Ginsburg joins this election-specific explanation without adopting Finley's broader spending discussion. Stone-Zsela reaches the federal question in dissent; he supplies no additional join in the lead's adequate-independent-state-ground explanation.

#### Controlling Propositions and Authority

##### 1. The federal question is reviewable

**Holding and operative rule:** Section 1257 permits review of the federal constitutional holding where the state court expressly treats the relevant state constitutional protection as coextensive and supplies no adequate independent state ground sustaining its judgment. The Court may decide this federal challenge without announcing an independent construction of Florida's Constitution.

**Authority:** Stevens's Part I is joined by all seven other Associates; eight direct rationale votes.

**Controlling explanation:** The Florida Supreme Court sustained the allocation against the federal challenge and resolved the parallel state claim on the same protection. Its stated state-law treatment therefore does not insulate the federal holding from review. The Court addresses that holding alone and leaves broader questions of Florida constitutional law undecided.

**Precedent treatment:** No earlier Supreme Court rule is altered; the ordinary federal-review and independent-state-ground boundaries apply.

##### 2. This objective support criterion is constitutional at the demonstrated burden

**Holding and operative rule:** A State may allocate this limited party-expense benefit according to an objective five-percent registered-support criterion where lawfully collected fees, continued candidate access, unrestricted private political spending and the demonstrated record establish no severe associational burden, and the measure reasonably serves stable public participation. The holding permits demonstrated-support financing; it does not permit preserving named incumbents or suppressing political viewpoints as independent objectives.

**Authority:** Stevens's Part II is joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; eight direct rationale votes, including the stated limitations.

**Controlling explanation:** Anderson v. Celebrezze requires comparing the character and magnitude of actual injury with the State's precise interests and their need for the burden. Burdick v. Takushi applies that inquiry to the complete electoral setting: severe burdens demand narrowly fitted compelling justification; reasonable, nondiscriminatory burdens ordinarily may rest on important regulatory interests. A funding label does not excuse examination of the classification, but a comparative benefit alone does not establish severe restriction.

Buckley v. Valeo, Part III, permits demonstrated-support conditions on election funding and distinguishes withholding a subsidy from excluding a candidacy. Here the objective, potentially changing registration threshold reasonably measures stable party support. Supporting established public participation without subsidizing every splinter organization is a legitimate allocation interest. Wilson's individual ballot qualification does not establish an automatic entitlement to party-wide financial assistance. Norman v. Reed protects independently qualified candidacies; this provision does not remove one from the ballot.

The strongest contrary argument is that selective aid magnifies existing parties' advantages after rivals qualify. Such an allocation remains reviewable for substantial suppression, viewpoint favoritism or discriminatory administration. This record establishes no such burden beyond the limited benefit's existence. Florida's registration measure differs from Buckley's vote criteria, expenditure ceilings and post-election payments; those features are not imported here. The Court does not adopt unqualified rhetoric about discouraging minor parties, a general rational-basis exemption for funding, or validity for every five-percent threshold.

**Precedent treatment:**

- Anderson applies the actual-burden and precise-interest inquiry to this financial classification.
- Burdick preserves burden-sensitive scrutiny; its write-in presumption is not transferred to all subsidies.
- Buckley supplies demonstrated-support funding authority while retaining constitutional limits and political fluidity; the schemes are not identical.
- Norman preserves qualified-component ballot protection without creating automatic party-expense funding.
- Arkansas Educational Television Commission v. Forbes preserves review of genuine support criteria and viewpoint discrimination; its forum classification is not an election-finance rule.
- National Endowment for the Arts v. Finley supplies no universal subsidy immunity; its arts-program holding and divided spending rationales retain their actual scope.

##### 3. Affirmance supplies no new payment or allocation entitlement

**Holding and operative rule:** Because the presented federal challenge fails, the judgment sustaining §99.103(1)'s limited allocation is affirmed without a rebate, refund or judicially prescribed formula. The lawful collection of candidate fees, access to the ballot and a materially different source-of-funds exaction remain outside the adjudicated challenge.

**Authority:** Stevens's Part III is joined by all seven other Associates; eight direct rationale votes.

**Controlling explanation:** The challengers sought relief against discriminatory operation of the allocation, while conceding lawful fee collection. The Court's bounded constitutional conclusion supplies no basis for enjoining this scheme or directing new payments. No state-law refund claim, expenditure ceiling or future financing system is decided.

**Precedent treatment:** Buckley remains a source of lawful financing distinctions, not a command to adopt its formula or award money in this case.

#### Precedent Treatment

- Anderson v. Celebrezze: applies the actual injury, precise interest and necessary-burden inquiry.
- Burdick v. Takushi: retains scrutiny according to actual burden; no universal funding exemption or write-in presumption for subsidies is created.
- Buckley v. Valeo: applies demonstrated-support financing principles while distinguishing its particular vote criteria, recipient expenditure ceilings and post-election payments.
- Norman v. Reed: preserves independently qualified candidacies without equating candidate qualification with every party subsidy.
- Arkansas Educational Television Commission v. Forbes: retains reasonable actual selection and viewpoint review within its forum setting; neither its majority nor its dissent supplies automatic subsidy access.
- National Endowment for the Arts v. Finley: retains its narrow arts holding and separately supported spending discussion; no broader subsidy rationale is attributed to the full Court here.

#### Law After Decision

Florida's limited, objective party-expense allocation survives this federal challenge on the demonstrated record. Public election assistance may distinguish demonstrated party support without automatically following every candidate's ballot qualification. Actual burdens, viewpoint manipulation and discriminatory administration remain reviewable; neither established-party preservation for its own sake nor the funding label ends constitutional scrutiny. No monetary entitlement or general validity for five-percent thresholds results.

#### Separate Writings

**Stone-Zsela, dissenting.** Stone-Zsela would reverse because this mandatory candidate-fee allocation gives an institutional benefit to established parties while withholding the same form of support from a recognized smaller party whose candidate has already qualified and paid the lawful fee. Anderson and Burdick require examination of that injury and Florida's actual interest. The five-percent statewide-registration threshold measures accumulated party strength rather than this candidate's qualified race or an identified administrative cost of returning the fee. For him, preserving established organizations and avoiding factional alternatives do not adequately justify this particular exclusion; institutional advantage cannot be its own constitutional end.

Buckley permits genuine support-sensitive financing and is not overruled by that position. Norman reinforces that unrelated party-organization restrictions cannot nullify valid candidate qualification, though Stone-Zsela does not claim the challenged rule literally removes Wilson from the ballot. The party asserts the participation interests of its members and voters, not personal rights for every legal entity. Collection and distribution of fees are government action; total ballot exclusion is unnecessary for constitutional review. No finding that minor-party payments were directly transferred to rivals is needed for his objection to the different benefits generated by the same type of lawful fee.

He would enjoin further distribution under the invalid classification after orderly implementation on remand. Florida could end the rebate, extend it evenhandedly to recognized parties with qualified candidates, or adopt a genuine support-sensitive measure justified by an independent constitutional interest. He would require no repayment of completed distributions and create no unrestricted entitlement to public money, guarantee of every minor party's survival, or obligation to finance every prospective candidate. His proposed invalidation does not command a majority.

The [Florida Supreme Court opinion, 687 So. 2d 1292](https://static.case.law/so2d/687/html/1292-01.html) and [First District opinion, 665 So. 2d 1119](https://static.case.law/so2d/665/html/1119-01.html) supply the statutory operation, lawful-fee concession, candidate qualification and review posture. [Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1, Part III](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/424/1) supplies the received public-financing discussion. The original petitions and full statutory editions are not reproduced in the available public sources; neither the exact petition wording nor an exact dollar-allocation formula is reproduced there. The decision addresses the bounded scheme described in the published sources.

#### Mandate, Remedy, and Stage

The Florida Supreme Court judgment stands on the federal question. No new funding, refund, ballot placement, allocation formula or administrative timetable is ordered. The Court leaves unpresented state-law entitlements and materially different future applications undecided.

**End of entry: Libertarian Party of Florida v. Smith, Plenary merits decision on submission, September 21, 1998.**
